section_summary: This section comprises diplomatic despatches, memoranda, letters, cross-reference sheets, and military intelligence reports concerning Japanese internal politics, foreign affairs, and army radicalism in early 1936 following the February 26 Incident. Major topics include Ambassador Grew's analysis of the newly formed Hirota Cabinet's platform and public reception, public inquiries regarding Christian reformer Toyohiko Kagawa, an analysis of the root causes of the February 26 insurrection, and the appointment of Hachiro Arita as Foreign Minister. It also features extensive coverage of the court-martial of Lieutenant Colonel Saburo Aizawa for the August 1935 assassination of Lieutenant General Tetsuzan Nagata, highlighting intense factional strife, ideological justifications, and unrest within the Japanese armed forces.

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew analyzes the policy declaration of the newly formed Hirota Cabinet, assessing planned economic and administrative reforms, military demands, positive foreign policy toward the USSR and China, and domestic press commentary, with two attached newspaper clippings.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew concludes Despatch No. 1733 from Tokyo examining the platform of Premier Koki Hirota's Cabinet in the aftermath of the February 26 Incident. The despatch evaluates proposals for clarifying the national polity, taxation readjustment, state control of key industries, and administrative reorganizations driven by the military. It surveys domestic press reactions, noting that the cabinet is widely viewed as a compromise dependent on the Army, and encloses two newspaper clippings detailing Hirota's policy declaration and the War Ministry's structural demands.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1733: Statement of Policy of the Hirota Cabinet and Reactions of the Japanese Public, Press, and Military

subfiles.about: A Minnesota lawyer inquires with Assistant Secretary of State Sayre about the impact of Toyohiko Kagawa's pacifist writings on the Japanese populace.
subfiles.summary: W. B. Taylor, an attorney in Grand Rapids, Minnesota, writes to Assistant Secretary of State Francis B. Sayre following his reading of William Axling's biography of Toyohiko Kagawa. Taylor suggests that if Kagawa's writings have been absorbed by the Japanese people, the United States has little to fear from Japanese aggression. He asks whether the State Department can provide information on the actual effect of Kagawa's works in Japan.
subfiles.title: Letter from W. B. Taylor to Assistant Secretary of State Francis B. Sayre Regarding Toyohiko Kagawa

subfiles.about: Assistant Secretary Sayre replies to W. B. Taylor concerning the difficulty of evaluating the societal influence of Toyohiko Kagawa's writings in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Assistant Secretary of State Francis B. Sayre replies to W. B. Taylor's letter regarding the influence of Toyohiko Kagawa in Japan. Sayre explains that assessing the effect of an author's writings on a population as large and varied as Japan's involves too many imponderables for the Department to provide an official opinion. He suggests that Taylor seek the views of private individuals who have lived in Japan to obtain firsthand insights.
subfiles.title: Letter from Assistant Secretary of State Francis B. Sayre to W. B. Taylor

subfiles.about: A Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizes Tokyo Embassy despatches analyzing the root causes, military indiscipline, and key events of the February 26 Incident.
subfiles.summary: W. T. Turner of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs prepares a memorandum for Under Secretary William Phillips summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 1718 by Erle R. Dickover on the factors behind the February 26 uprising. The memorandum outlines fundamental causes, including agrarian distress, ideological conflict over the Emperor's position, army indiscipline, the Aizawa court-martial, and dissatisfaction with foreign policy. It also calls attention to an appended memorandum of conversation with Dr. James A. Scherer regarding General Jinzaburo Mazaki and references Despatch No. 1721 detailing the chronology of events.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Tokyo Incident of February 26 by Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: A register lists twenty telegrams transmitted by the American Embassy in Tokyo to the Department of State throughout February 1935.
subfiles.summary: This document is a tabular index of telegrams sent from the American Embassy in Tokyo to the Department of State between February 2 and February 27, 1935. It catalogs telegram numbers 22 through 41 along with their dates, transmission times, and subject matters. Recorded subjects include Sino-Japanese negotiations, the Manchurian oil monopoly, arrests of American businessmen in Osaka, Japanese naval plans, and oil concessions in Portuguese Timor.
subfiles.title: Telegrams Sent to the Department During February, 1935

subfiles.about: A Department cross-reference sheet records Tokyo telegram No. 84 reporting the appointment of Hachiro Arita as Minister for Foreign Affairs.
subfiles.summary: This State Department document file note serves as an index sheet cross-referencing decimal file 894.00/641 to 894.002/284. It documents Telegram No. 84 received from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo, dated April 4, 1936. The record notes the appointment of Hachiro Arita as Minister for Foreign Affairs and confirms that he assumed office on April 2, 1936.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Appointment of Hachiro Arita as Minister for Foreign Affairs

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports by telegram the appointment of Hachiro Arita as Minister for Foreign Affairs.
subfiles.summary: In confidential Telegram No. 84 from Tokyo, Ambassador Joseph C. Grew informs the Secretary of State that Hachiro Arita, recently Ambassador to China, has been appointed Minister for Foreign Affairs. Grew confirms that Arita took office on the evening of April 2, 1936. He also refers the Department to a confidential biographical report on Arita transmitted previously on March 2.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 84 Regarding Appointment of Foreign Minister Hachiro Arita

subfiles.about: Military Attaché Major William C. Crane reports on the court-martial of Lieutenant Colonel Saburo Aizawa for the assassination of Lieutenant General Tetsuzan Nagata, transmitting extensive press clippings covering the proceedings.
subfiles.summary: Major William C. Crane, Assistant Military Attaché in Tokyo, forwards Report No. 8187 to the War Department regarding the first court-martial of Lieutenant Colonel Saburo Aizawa for the August 12, 1935 murder of Lieutenant General Tetsuzan Nagata. Crane observes that the trial was interrupted past legal limits by the February 26 Incident, requiring a new trial to be convened, and remarks on the extensive latitude allowed to the defense to air radical nationalist grievances. Attached clippings from The Japan Advertiser (January 29, January 31, and February 7, 1936) provide comprehensive accounts of the open court sessions, including Aizawa's testimony on his motives, defense arguments by Lieutenant Colonel Sakichi Mitsui, petitions written in blood, and descriptions of the assassination scene in the War Ministry.
subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report No. 8187: Court-Martial of Lieutenant Colonel Saburo Aizawa with Attached Press Clippings
